I'm researching linux more and more and trying to figure out what exactly the difference between linux distros is. It looks like it's the pre-included software, the desktop environment, and the software repository. If you change the last two things, then are you basically using a different distro?
Not counting included software, if you change the DE and Repository to a distro that matches them, are you basically using that distro then?

Well...not exactly....

The DE is not really that important for what makes a distro a distro...almost all distros allow you installing a alternative DE. They just have one default DE.

And you can't switch to a repository of another distro. The reason for this is....much more what makes the differences between distros. Not sure how to explain this...so let me try. Programs have dependencies...for example almost all programs displaying an png image in the end rely on libpng to load the file. The program itself has no code to load a png file an rather uses libpng. This allows reusing the same code in plenty of programs...and has a lot of advantages. For example if a security issue is found in libpng it only needs to replace that one library and all programs using it are safe again.

But it also has some disadvantages. The sourcecode of programs is pretty tolerant against very small changes in such libraries..only really major updates will make changes to the source code necessary. But this is not true for compiled programs. One part of the compile process deals with how functions from an external library are called. For this it builds kind of a table with addresses to those functions. And here comes the problem....it is very, very simple to mess up that table...only a small change in the library can do that. This means that compiled programs are compiled against a specific version of a library...it's more luck if they run with a different version.

This gets even more complicated as distros can choose what options of the sourcecode to include in their programs/libraries. A lot libraries and programs allow configuration on source code level...like what graphical toolkits they support or what databases. Distros make those choices for their repositories....but they are not the same choice another distro makes. But that means of course that other programs depending on such a library can have exceptions what features are enabled and which disabled. Inside the repository of one distro that is never a problem...the distro makes sure all fits. But it makes mixing of repositories of different distros impossible. And if you can't mix repositories you also can't change from one to another...your package manage would fail as soon as one of it's dependencies gets replaced with a incompatible one.

Over all...different distros are different OSes. The differences are in how their packages are configured and also in what choices they make for packages that have alternatives.

(all that is for different distros...with derivatives like mint or elementary this is not as bad as they are basically still ubuntu just with some changes on a very high level)
Great answer, thanks a lot. I wasn't aware you couldn't change repositories and they all followed a different source code.

Choosing to use Kubuntu over Ubuntu is still using Ubuntu. It's not a different distro, it's just different packages. Choosing to use Funtoo instead of using Ubuntu would be choosing a different distro. So if you were to have Ubuntu running and decide you want to use LXDE instead of Unity, then you're still using Ubuntu just with LXDE.

Package management, dependency resolution and defaults are really the only major differences between distros.

Culture is the other thing. Debian wants to be stable, Arch wants to be bleeding edge, Redhat wants to be corporate. Different cultures drive what each distro holds dear.

But yeah, if you have the same defaults as CentOS, use the same repos and use RPM, you're basically CentOS.
